stories.headline: FED HEADS INTO TUESDAY-WEDNESDAY MEETING WITH HIKE ODDS NEAR 85%
stories.body: The FOMC meets Tuesday and Wednesday, with a decision due Wednesday at 2 PM ET alongside a fresh Summary of Economic Projections and dot plot. Market-implied odds of a quarter-point hike sit near 85% following Friday's hotter-than-expected core CPI print, even as softer July hiring and retail-sales data keep a hold scenario alive.
stories.explain: The September meeting is one of four each year that comes with a Summary of Economic Projections, so Wednesday's release carries more information than the rate decision alone: the dot plot shows each policymaker's anonymous rate forecast for year-end and beyond, and shifts in the median dot function as guidance for where policy is headed even when the current move is already priced in. That's why a hike that's 85% expected can still move markets sharply if the dots signal a shallower or steeper path than investors assumed.

stories.headline: HOUTHI FORCES SEIZE YEMENI PORT OF MOCHA, SAUDI SHUTS KEY PIPELINE AFTER ATTACKS
stories.body: Iran-backed Houthi forces captured the Yemeni port city of Mocha over the weekend, tightening their grip near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, while Saudi Arabia's energy ministry confirmed it shut down a cross-country pipeline as a precaution after Thursday's attacks. Markets are closed until Monday, but the developments layer fresh supply-risk premium on top of Friday's already-elevated WTI level near $100.
stories.explain: Oil traders price geopolitical chokepoints on probability, not on actual barrels interrupted — a captured port near a strait carrying a meaningful share of global crude flows raises the implied odds of a disruption even before any tanker is turned away. That's the same mechanism that pushed WTI toward $104 last week before Friday's partial retreat, and it makes Monday's open a real test of whether markets treat this weekend's escalation as incremental risk or a genuine supply threat.

stories.headline: WHITE HOUSE ESCALATES CANADA TARIFFS: 50% LEVY MONDAY, BROADER BAN LATE SEPTEMBER
stories.body: A 50% U.S. tariff on Canadian goods including mattresses, motorboats, and golf carts takes effect Monday, Sept. 15, with a separate ban on Canadian dairy, most alcohol, and motorcycles set to begin Sept. 29. Canadian retailers are already relabeling shelves as a "buy Canadian" boycott reshapes grocery purchasing north of the border.
stories.explain: A tariff functions as a tax on the importer, and the incidence — how much gets passed to the end consumer versus absorbed by margins — depends on how substitutable the good is; a golf cart or motorboat has few close domestic substitutes at scale, so expect most of that 50% to show up in shelf prices rather than importer margins. The dairy and alcohol ban is a different tool entirely — a quantity restriction rather than a price one — and tends to show up as a supply gap and higher category-specific prices rather than a broad inflation print.

stories.headline: STOCKS CLOSE OUT THE WEEK STRONG HEADING INTO A HEAVY CATALYST CALENDAR
stories.body: Friday's close left the S&P 500 at 7,657 (+0.86%) and the Nasdaq-100 at 29,368 (+0.91%), both snapping a four-session slide, heading into a week that stacks the FOMC decision, the BOJ meeting, and a new tariff deadline inside five trading days. Gold added 0.49% to $4,366 even as the dollar index slipped 0.03% to 99.12.
stories.explain: Markets typically discount known catalysts individually, but when several land in the same week — a live Fed decision, a foreign central bank hike, and a tariff deadline — realized volatility tends to run higher than any single-event pricing would suggest, because dealers must hedge against multiple simultaneous scenarios rather than one. That's part of why implied volatility gauges tend to tick up heading into weeks like this one, even before any of the actual news arrives.

stories.headline: BANK OF JAPAN SET TO HIKE TO 1.25% THURSDAY, ADDING TO GLOBAL TIGHTENING PUSH
stories.body: Economists surveyed are nearly unanimous that the Bank of Japan will raise its policy rate 25 basis points to 1.25% at its Sept. 17-18 meeting, continuing the tightening path that began with the end of decades of near-zero rates. The BOJ decision lands just a day after the Fed's own move, giving global rates markets two central-bank catalysts within the same week.
stories.explain: Japan has historically been the world's largest exporter of cheap capital — Japanese investors borrow yen at low rates and buy higher-yielding assets abroad in what's called the carry trade — so a BOJ hike raises the cost of that funding leg and can pull capital back toward yen assets. When that unwind happens quickly, as it did in August 2024, it can spill into global equity and currency volatility well beyond Japan, which is why a widely expected 25bp move still gets flagged as a risk event.

stories.headline: FLORIDA, ILLINOIS HEADLINE PRESEASON TOP 25 AS TRANSFER PORTAL RESHAPES CONTENDERS
stories.body: Florida checks in at No. 1 in CBS Sports' preseason Top 25 And 1, projected to return six of its top seven scorers from last season's SEC champion and No. 1 NCAA Tournament seed, while Illinois debuts at No. 2 in FOX Sports' poll — the Illini's highest preseason ranking since 1985 — after a wave of transfer additions. North Carolina, Missouri, and Gonzaga also landed notable portal hauls as programs finalize rosters ahead of November tip-off.

stories.headline: NBA STRIPS CLIPPERS OF FIVE FIRST-ROUND PICKS, FINES BALLMER $30 MILLION
stories.body: The NBA concluded its investigation into alleged salary-cap circumvention tied to Kawhi Leonard and stripped the Los Angeles Clippers of five first-round draft picks while fining owner Steve Ballmer $30 million, one of the harshest penalties in league history. The ruling reshapes the Clippers' asset base for the rest of the decade, in a week that also saw Trail Blazers guard Shaedon Sharpe go down with a torn meniscus expected to cost him roughly six months.

stories.headline: PACKERS RB JOSH JACOBS REMAINS ON COMMISSIONER'S EXEMPT LIST AS LEGAL CASE PLAYS OUT
stories.body: Green Bay running back Josh Jacobs opened the season on the NFL's commissioner's exempt list following a May arrest on domestic-violence-related charges that were later reduced to two misdemeanors — battery and criminal damage to property. Jacobs continues to draw his salary but cannot practice or play until the league lifts the designation; his initial court date is Nov. 17, and any time already spent on the list would count toward a future suspension.

stories.headline: TEXAS STUNS NO. 1 OHIO STATE 24-23, ERASING 20-POINT FOURTH-QUARTER DEFICIT
stories.body: No. 4 Texas rallied from a 20-point fourth-quarter hole to beat top-ranked Ohio State 24-23 in Austin, the first time since 2004 that an AP No. 1 has lost after leading by 20-plus points that late in a game (previously 197-0). The result vaults Texas to No. 1 in the new Week 3 poll and drops Ohio State to No. 6, on the same weekend Oklahoma State upset then-No. 6 Oregon and Michigan knocked off Oklahoma.

Rutgers transfer Harun Zrno and Texas Tech transfer LeJuan Watts (11.8 ppg last season) continue to round out Danny Sprinkle's roster; UW's non-conference slate includes a marquee matchup with Baylor at Climate Pledge Arena.

deepDive.title: What the Fed's Dot Plot Actually Measures — And Why Wednesday Matters More Than the Rate Itself
content: Tuesday and Wednesday's FOMC meeting is drawing attention almost entirely to whether the committee hikes 25 basis points, with market pricing near 85% in favor. But the September meeting is one of four each year that also releases the Summary of Economic Projections, commonly known as the dot plot, and that document usually moves markets more than the rate decision itself when the decision is this widely expected. Understanding what the dot plot is — and isn't — measuring is the difference between reading Wednesday's headline and understanding what actually shifted underneath it.

Each of the FOMC's voting and non-voting participants submits an anonymous dot representing where they think the fed funds rate should sit at the end of the current year and each of the next few years, plus a longer-run estimate. The Fed plots all the dots on a scatter chart and reports the median — that median becomes shorthand for "the Fed's" rate path, even though it's really a set of individual, non-binding guesses updated only four times a year. A hike that's fully priced in moves nothing on its own; it's the median dot for 2027 shifting up or down by even a single quarter-point increment that resets the entire forward curve traders actually price off of.

In December 2018, the Fed hiked as expected but the dot plot signaled two more hikes for 2019 instead of the three markets had partially priced in — a seemingly small revision that helped trigger a nearly 20% stock selloff into Christmas Eve, before the Fed reversed course within weeks. The lesson wasn't that the Fed made a policy mistake; it was that a small change in a handful of anonymous guesses can outweigh the actual rate move that already happened, because markets discount decisions but re-price expectations in real time. Most casual market-watchers read the headline "Fed hikes" and miss this second, more consequential layer entirely.

This week's setup makes that second layer unusually loaded: an 85%-priced hike gives the committee cover to either validate a hawkish path if core inflation stays sticky, or signal a pause if July's softer labor and retail data carry more weight behind closed doors than Friday's CPI beat suggested publicly. With the Bank of Japan hiking three days later and a fresh Canada tariff deadline landing the same week, Wednesday's dot plot won't just set the tone for U.S. rates — it will be read as the Fed's answer to whether this week's stacked catalysts are net inflationary or net growth-slowing.
